steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
When the storms came in from the north, the whole island shrank to the circle of light.

Elias turned the lantern lens with both hands, feeling the familiar resistance of brass and glass. The great Fresnel lens—fifty years old, older than he was—ticked as it revolved, sending its white blade of light out across the writhing sea. The foghorn bellowed, low and mournful, every thirty seconds like the slow breathing of some slumbering beast.

He checked the watch in his vest pocket. 1:17 a.m.

The logbook lay open on the desk beside the window, its pages filled with his neat, crabbed handwriting. He wrote, as he did every night:

“0130. Wind NNE, rising. Visibility poor.
Light functioning properly.
Keeper on duty.”

He had added that last line the day after Marianne died.

For thirty years they had kept the light together. She had scrubbed the brass and polished the glass; he had tended the flame and mended the stairs. When the batteries came, then the diesel generator, then the halogen lamp, they had learned each new system side by side. Marianne had joked that they were already ghosts, bound to the tower like the keepers in the old stories, condemned to walk the stairs until the sea swallowed them whole.

But death came quietly, in early spring, in the little bedroom on the second floor, and left Elias with a silence that clung to the stone.

He climbed the last steps to the lantern room and stepped out into the circular glass cage. Rain hissed against the panes. The sea beyond was black and turbulent, its only hints of motion caught where the beam dragged over whitecaps. He checked the oil levels out of habit, though the light had been electric for decades now. Some routines you kept because they worked; others you kept because without them, too much would fall apart.

Down the coast, twelve nautical miles away, the town’s lights were a distant orange smudge. They had built a new harbor two years ago, with navigation buoys and electronic charts and pilots who talked to ships by satellite and radio. The men from the Authority had come in a neat white boat and told him—politely, apologetically—that the lighthouse was now “supplemental.” The word had landed like a stone in his chest.

“Shipping has changed, Mr. Vance,” the younger one had said, glancing at his clipboard instead of at Elias. “The big vessels track by GPS now. We’re automating most of the remaining lights. The keepers are retiring.”

“Lights fail,” Elias had replied. “Batteries drain. Storms scramble signals. You ever seen a trawler captain in a whiteout with a dead radio?”

The young man had shifted his weight, uncomfortable, as though such images had never entered his orderly life.

“Of course, of course,” he’d said. “That’s why the light will remain operational. It’s just that it will be… remotely monitored. Along with the others.”

When Elias didn’t answer right away, the older inspector had stepped forward, softer around the eyes.

“We’ll place you in town,” he’d said. “You’d be comfortable there. No need to climb these stairs every day. Medical services close by.”

Elias had looked past them, to where Marianne’s garden still clung stubbornly to the lee side of the island—a few scraggly rosebushes, a stubborn rosemary, the half-collapsed trellis where she’d once tried to coax beans to grow in the salt air. The idea of leaving felt like abandoning something that could not leave with him.

“I’ll stay until it’s done,” he’d said at last. “Until they turn it over to your machine.”

They’d exchanged a quick glance and, seeing no harm in humoring an old man, agreed.

That was fourteen months ago. The generator still coughed to life when he cranked it. The beam still swept the horizon with patient regularity. The Authority sent fuel and supplies once a month; young men in red jackets hauled crates up from the boathouse and left as quickly as weather allowed.

None of them stayed long enough to notice that Elias always checked the lens first, even before the fresh bread or the mail.

He made his next round just after two. Down the spiral stairs he went, one hand on the cool iron rail, his boots landing on each worn stone in a pattern his muscles knew better than his mind. On the service level he checked pressure, listened to the grind and hum of the machinery. Everything in order.

In the kitchen, the old wall clock ticked with a sound far too large for its size. Elias warmed his hands around a mug of tea gone lukewarm. The wind shoved at the windows, and spray rattled like thrown gravel.

He was halfway through his second sip when the radio crackled.

“—questing bearing—…damn thing— Hello, coast station, this is the fishing vessel Marlin’s Luck, one-two miles off Northpoint, visibility near zero. Anyone reading?”

The voice was tight at the edges in a way that told Elias more than the words. He set down his mug and crossed to the radio, flicking the transmit switch with a practiced thumb.

“Marlin’s Luck, this is Northpoint Light,” he said. His voice emerged steady, though his heart had begun to thud in a different rhythm. “I read you. What’s your situation?”

There was a brief hiss of static, then an audible exhale of relief.

“Northpoint, good to hear someone. Our GPS went dark an hour back. Nothing but snow on the screen now. We thought we were running south along the coast, but I can’t see a thing out here. Radar’s a mess in this rain. I was hoping for your light, but the fog is thick as soup. Can’t get a fix.”

Elias glanced toward the window. From here the beam’s flash painted faint ghosts on the low clouds, but down at sea level, with the fog rolling in, it might well be swallowed entirely.

“State your last known position,” he said. “And your heading.”

The numbers came back after a moment’s fumbling. Elias reached for the worn chart hung on the wall by two rusting nails, his fingers steady. The coastline unrolled before him in ink and contour lines, as familiar as the creases of his own palm.

“You’re closer to us than you think,” he said. “The current’s pushed you west. If you keep your present course, you’ll come up on Needle Rock inside the half hour.”

Silence, then a low curse over the open channel.

“Thought we were well off that,” the captain muttered. The strain in his voice had deepened. “Can’t see a blessed thing. If we swing farther out, we risk running blind into the shipping lane.”

“Listen carefully,” Elias said. “I’ll sound the horn at thirty-second intervals. Steer so the horn stays off your starboard bow, never ahead of you. That will keep you clear of the shoals. When the beam becomes visible, you’re to keep it dead ahead until I tell you otherwise. Do you copy?”

Another pause. Someone in the background said something he couldn’t make out.

“Copy that, Northpoint. Steering to keep your horn starboard. Appreciate the help. It’s… good to hear the old tower’s still manned.”

“Light’s burning,” Elias replied. “Stand by.”

He set the radio down and went to the foghorn controls. The automation could sound it, true, on a set pattern when fog density reached a preset level. But tonight he dialed in a manual override, fingers moving over the panel more from feel than sight. He’d use the horn as a voice, as men had before electronics came.

The first blast shook the stones under his feet.

Every thirty seconds, the tower gave that long, guttural bellow. Elias timed them with the clock, listening between each for the distant thud of engines, the shape of the storm.

Minutes stretched, each one heavy. On the chart, he traced a likely path the Marlin’s Luck would be taking now, tacking by sound instead of sight, his palm flattened against the paper to feel some echo of their movement.

After ten minutes, the radio hissed again.

“Northpoint, this is Marlin’s Luck. We have your horn off our starboard, faint but clear. Still no visual on the light. Seas are getting rougher. We’re trusting your word here.”

“Hold your course,” Elias said. He could hear the swell in the distance, the deep rumble under the wind. Somewhere out there, a steel hull rose and fell, men squinting into nothing. “You’re clear of Needle Rock now. When you sight the beam, shout out immediately. Don’t assume it means you’re safe.”

A burst of laughter came through, too sharp to be entirely genuine.

“Understood, lighthouse. No one’s assuming anything tonight.”

He left the radio on and climbed again. His legs complained in a dull way that meant he’d feel it in the morning, but there was a lighter note in the ache, like the memory of long-gone nights when he and Marianne had run up and down these stairs together, racing the clock, racing each other.

In the lantern room, the wind had become a high, angry whine. The glass shuddered now and then as a particularly strong gust hurled rain against it. The beam went on turning, patient and indifferent, writing its slow circle over the world.

Elias opened the narrow door to the gallery and stepped out into the storm.

Salt and water slapped his face. The island was gone beneath him, the black drop of the cliff invisible beyond the railing, but he knew exactly where its edge waited. He gripped the metal rail and leaned out, peering into the murk.

White noise everywhere: wind, water, the internal roar of his own blood. Below that, if he focused, the faint thrum of engines, there then swallowed again.

He had stood on this gallery in storms worse than this, felt the tower lean like a ship and spring back. He had watched lightning turn the sea to molten white, watched rogue waves strike the base with a force that shook dust from the rafters. Those nights, Marianne had waited just inside, holding a towel, muttering that one day the sea would simply decide it had had enough of their stubbornness and take the whole island in one bite.

He closed his eyes now and listened. The horn bellowed behind his shoulder; its echo came back from the cliff face with a slight delay he knew by heart. Between those calls, the distant engine grew slowly, almost imperceptibly, louder.

Then, through the sheet of rain, he saw it: a faint, ghostly smudge of yellow, then the clearer, more resolute glow of his own light on the underside of low clouds.

A few seconds later, the radio crackled.

“Northpoint! We’ve got you. Light dead ahead. Sweet mercy, that’s a sight.”

“Do not put it astern,” Elias said immediately, ducking back inside. His fingers left wet streaks on the glass of the lantern room as he moved to the chart table. “In ten minutes, you’re to alter course ten degrees port. Repeat that back.”

The numbers came, correct. He could hear the crew talking over each other now, a babble blurred by static. In his mind’s eye, he saw them: rain-slicked decks, wet ropes, eyes squinted against stinging salt, one hand on the wheel, the other white-knuckled on a rail.

He rode with them in his thoughts as they adjusted course, counting down the minutes, the flashes of his own light ticking them forward.

At last, after a series of small course corrections, the captain’s voice came again, and this time it carried something new: the fragile buoyancy of relief that had not yet had time to settle.

“Northpoint, this is Marlin’s Luck. Our radar’s clearing up. We’re showing clear water all around. Seas still heavy but bottom depth is good. Plotting on the chart puts us right where you said we’d be, clear past Needle Rock and well off the shoals.”

Elias let out a breath he hadn’t realized he’d been holding.

“Then you’re past the worst,” he said simply. “Keep the light on your quarter now and you’ll ride safely down the coast. The harbor will take you the rest of the way.”

There was a pause, then the captain said, more quietly, “Couldn’t have done it without you, Northpoint. Thought they’d automated your old place by now.”

“Not yet,” Elias said. He glanced at the lens, at the steady rotation of gears and glass. “Tonight it’s still got hands on it.”

“Well, from all of us aboard, thank you. We’ll send a bottle your way when the seas calm.”

“Save your fuel,” Elias replied. “Just get home.”

The radio clicked off. The absence of the captain’s voice left behind a deeper resonance in the room, as if something that had been stretched taut had released.

He stayed awake until dawn, watching the beam carve its measured path, listening to the storm spend itself against the stubborn stone. The sky lightened from black to leaden gray, then to the faintest suggestion of blue at the ragged horizon. When the first thread of the sun slid under the clouds, he shut off the lamp.

For a long moment, the sudden dimness made the lantern room seem smaller. Without the bright rotation, it was merely a glass room atop an aging tower, and he only an old man with aching knees and a shirt damp from the night’s exertions.

He descended to the kitchen and warmed his tea again. Outside, the sea was a different creature now—still restless, but no longer furious, its whitecaps catching new light. Gulls wheeled and shrieked, indignant at the interruption of their usual morning squabbles.

On the table lay the Authority’s last letter, its logo crisp at the top, its language as careful and inevitable as the turning of seasons.

“Automation schedule confirmed. Remote control installation to commence September 12. Lighthouse to be unmanned thereafter.”

He had read it three times when it came, his eyes stopping each time on that last word: unmanned. As if the stone and glass and steel could care one way or the other. As if the light reduced to a thing that simply switched on and off at the right times, indifferent to fog, to storms, to men’s voices on the edge of fear.

He picked up the letter again, then set it aside. He took the logbook instead and wrote:

“0645. Storm passed. Assisted Marlin’s Luck in clearing Needle Rock. Light and horn in continuous operation. Keeper on duty.”

He paused, the pen hovering. Then, in smaller letters below, he added:

“For now.”

That afternoon, when the sun finally burned through the last of the low cloud, a small vessel approached from the south. Elias watched from the gallery as it rounded the point: white hull, bright orange stripe, the Authority’s mark on its side. Two men and a woman in hard hats and windbreakers stood on the deck with a crate between them, all crisp efficiency and modern paint.

They came ashore at the little landing, their voices thin on the wind. The younger man he recognized from the last visit; the older inspector was not among them this time. A shame, Elias thought, without quite knowing why.

They climbed the path, carrying cases of instruments, cables coiled like sleeping snakes.

“Mr. Vance,” the young man said when they reached him, slightly out of breath but trying not to show it. “Good to see you. We’ve come to install the remote control systems, as scheduled.”

Elias nodded. “You’ll want the generator room first,” he said. “Then the control board on the service level.”

They blinked, slightly surprised at his swift acquiescence, perhaps expecting argument, some small performance of rage or refusal. But the night’s work had settled something in him.

He led them inside. They commented on the neatness of the place, the good condition of the machinery. The woman—her name was Dr. Kellan, she said, an engineer—ran a hand over the brass fittings of the old lamp housing.

“It’s beautiful craftsmanship,” she murmured. “They don’t make them like this anymore.”

“Wouldn’t know how,” Elias said. “They weren’t built with planned obsolescence in mind.”

She smiled at that, faintly. Her hands were gentle as she affixed new sensors, threaded cables along the walls, mounted small, featureless boxes that would one day send silent signals inland.

It took them two days to complete the work. During that time, the light ran as always, the lens turning, the beam sweeping. On the third morning, they gathered at the control panel on the service level.

Dr. Kellan opened a waterproof case and removed a compact device with an antenna.

“We’ll send the first activation command from here,” she said. “Once the central station comes online, the light will be monitored continuously. If there’s a fault, they’ll know within seconds.”

“What if the line goes down?” Elias asked.

She hesitated, then said, “There are fail-safes. Local timers. Battery backups. The system is… robust.”

“Until it isn’t,” he said mildly.

Her expression flickered, then settled back into professional calm. “Until it isn’t, yes. But that’s true of any system, isn’t it?”

He thought of the Marlin’s Luck in the fog, of the relief in the captain’s voice when the light broke through.

“It is,” he conceded.

She pressed a button. Somewhere in the panel, a relay clicked. A small green light came on, reflecting in the curve of her safety glasses.

“There,” she said. “From this point on, the lamp can be powered and controlled remotely. We’ll leave the manual switch in place for now, as backup. But the Authority considers the station unmanned as of… today.”

Elias looked at the switch he’d thrown every sunset for three decades, the lever worn smooth where his thumb rested. Above it, someone had affixed a new label: REMOTE CONTROL ACTIVE.

He reached out and, without thinking, rubbed the corner of the label with his knuckle until the edge began to curl.

“You’ll have to sign here,” the young inspector said, offering a clipboard. “Acknowledging turnover.”

Elias took it. The page swam a little in his vision, and he had to adjust his spectacles. He signed his name where indicated. His hand did not tremble.

“Will you be going into town with us?” Dr. Kellan asked. “We can arrange accommodations while they finalize your pension arrangements.”

He imagined it: a small room in a square building, a window looking out over other windows instead of water. Streets that always ended in land. A horizon broken by roofs, not waves. People’s voices pressing close instead of the long, clean silence of sea and sky.

“I’ll come in on the supply boat, when it makes its usual run,” he said. “The island won’t vanish overnight. I’d like to put things in order.”

She studied him, then nodded once. “We’ll leave the keys in the usual place,” she said with the smallest hint of a smile, as if acknowledging some private code.

They left after lunch, their equipment packed away,
